latin_text: Dedignemur terrestria, caelestia contemnamus; et, quicquid mundi est denique posthabentes, ultramundanam curiam eminentissimae divinitati proximam advolemus. Ibi, ut sacra tradunt mysteria, Seraphin, Cherubin et Throni primas possident
english_translation: Let us spurn the terrestrial, disdain the celestial; disregarding all that is of this world, let us fly off to the otherworldly court that is near to the most eminent Divinity. There, according to the sacred mysteries, seraphim, cherubim, and thrones occupy the first places
exegesis:
[VERIFIED] Pico now invokes the celestial hierarchy explicitly, calling the reader to transcend all terrestrial and celestial knowledge and fly toward the transcendent unity-in-multiplicity (*ultramundanam curiam*) nearest the Godhead. The three highest angelic orders—Seraphim (the burning/loving ones), Cherubim (the knowledge-fullness), and Thrones (the steadfast powers)—occupy the supreme positions in the Pseudo-Dionysian hierarchy. [VERIFIED] This hierarchical theology derives from Pseudo-Dionysius's *Celestial Hierarchy* and has been systematized by Aquinas and the medieval scholastic tradition. Each order embodies a transcendent principle: Seraphim are the burning wheels of divine love, Cherubim the repositories of divine wisdom, Thrones the executors of divine justice and divine will.

The philosophical function is rhetorical and transformative: Pico addresses the reader directly, commanding the moral will toward transcendence (*dedignemur*, *contemnamus*, *advolemus*—let us spurn, disdain, fly off). The passage moves from the first and second cosmological passages (establishment of cosmos, human potential for ascent) to an urgent vocative: the transcendent goal is not merely intellectually available but existentially demanding. The reader is called to abandon all earthly and even all celestial attachments, to shed the weight of the cosmos itself, and to approach the Godhead in its transcendent otherness. The three highest orders are not distant mythological beings but accessible exemplars: the human who has cultivated love can align with Seraphim, the contemplative can share in Cherubic light, the just judge can participate in Throne-power.

[INFERRED] Heptaplus 6.6 elaborates the cosmological roles of these three orders. The Commento Book I establishes how they embody the three-fold structure of angelic intellection (undivided unity, multiplicative knowledge, judgment/causality). Being & Unity grounds them metaphysically as the highest forms of participated being—the closest creaturely approximations to the divine simplicity, unity, and transcendence.
notes: Pico calls for ascent beyond both earthly and celestial knowledge to the transcendent realm. He names the three highest orders of the Pseudo-Dionysian hierarchy: seraphim (love), cherubim (knowledge), thrones (will/judgment).
